newsitem.title: JAPAN: US Treasuries retain bullish sentiment in Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries retain bullish sentiment in Tokyo.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries remained firm by midday Tokyo on Friday, retaining strong sentiment after ending higher for the fourth straight day overnight, traders said.
Amid lingering bullish sentiment, traders see the next target for the yield of the key 30-year bond at 6.25 percent.

"117 (in the September T-bond futures contract) and 6.25 percent (of 30-year bond's yield) are in people's mind, and I think they will try to test those levels soon," a trader at a Japanese trust bank said.
He added that the recent rally may finally slow down once the market hits those targets.
The 6-5/8 percent 30-year bond was at 104-11/32 at 0309 GMT, yielding at 6.30 percent, compared with 104-10/32 at Thursday's New York close.
Meanwhile, the September T-bond futures contract was up 3/32 from the previous close to 116-27/32.
Traders said they will be closely watching the release of U.S. July nonfarm payrolls and unemployment data.

The average hourly earning is also largely focused on for hints of inflationary pressures. "Unless those figures show very shocking numbers, Treasuries will stay firm," a trader at a foreign brokerage house said.
In a Reuters survey, the consensus calls for payroll increase of 193,000 in July versus 217,000 in June, while the unemployment rate would edge down 0.1 percent to 4.9 percent.
As for average hourly earnings, the forecast of economists puts the figures up 0.2 percent in July versus June's up 0.3 percent.

"If the figures come out in line with market expectations, that will prompt more buying. And if the Treasuries end higher again (in New York), another strong rally is expected next week," the first trader said.

He added that even if economic indicators prove that the U.S. economy is in good shape and sparks profit-taking sales, traders, including Japanese players, who missed out on a chance to buy Treasuries at low prices, will be eager to buy on dips, keeping Treasuries firm.
